articles.title: Character.AI and Google settle teen suicide and self-harm suits
articles.summary: The companies reached agreements in several cases filed in courts across the country alleging their products harmed kids.
articles.body: Character.AI and Google have reached settlements with several families whose teens harmed themselves or died by suicide after interacting with Character.AI’s chatbots, according to new court filings. The details of the settlements are still unknown. The parties notified a federal court in Florida that they had reached a “mediated settlement in principle to resolve all claims,” and asked to pause the case to finalize the agreement. Character.AI spokesperson Kathryn Kelly, Google spokesperson Julie McAlister, and a lawyer from the Social Media Victims Law Center representing victims’ families, Matthew Bergman, declined to comment. The settled cases include a high-profile lawsuit filed by Megan Garcia, who claimed in an October 2024 complaint that Character.AI’s Game of Thrones-themed chatbot encouraged her 14-year-old son, Sewell Setzer, to go through with suicide after he had developed a “dependency” on the bot. The lawsuit said Google should be considered a “co-creator” of Character.AI because it “contributed financial resources, personnel, intellectual property, and AI technology,” to the tool, which was founded by former Google employees that the company later hired back. Following that lawsuit, Character.AI announced changes to its chatbot to safeguard users, including separating the large language model (LLM) for users under 18, to create an experience with stricter content restrictions, and adding parental controls. It later banned minors from open-ended character chats altogether. The companies also reached agreements in cases filed in Colorado, New York, and Texas, according to legal filings. The settlements will still need to be finalized and approved by the courts. Update, January 8th: Added a no comment from Matthew Bergman and Google spokesperson. --- If you or someone you know is considering suicide or is anxious, depressed, upset, or needs to talk, there are people who want to help. In the US: Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741-741 from anywhere in the US, at any time, about any type of crisis. 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988 (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline). The original phone number, 1-800-273-TALK (8255), is available as well. The Trevor Project: Text START to 678-678 or call 1-866-488-7386 at any time to speak to a trained counselor. Outside the US: The International Association for Suicide Prevention lists a number of suicide hotlines by country. Click here to find them. Befrienders Worldwide has a network of crisis helplines active in 48 countries. Click here to find them.

articles.title: ‘When You Say I Should Pay $100 Billion, Then I’m Starting To Do A Little Math’: Bill Gates Said He’d Happily Pay ‘Over $10 Billion In Taxes’ But Some Are Asking Too Much
articles.summary: Bill Gates says he is happy to pay taxes, but there should still be some limit.
articles.body:
On stage at the New York Times DealBook conference, Bill Gates was asked about Elizabeth Warren's wealth tax and answered by pointing to his own ledger. "I've paid over $10 billion in taxes. I've paid more than anyone in taxes," the Microsoft (MSFT) co-founder told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin. "If I had to pay $20 billion, it's fine. But when you say I should pay $100 billion, then I'm starting to do a little math about what I have left over." He added, a beat later: "Sorry, I'm just kidding."

The joke had a target. Warren was then running for the Democratic presidential nomination on an "Ultra-Millionaire Tax": a 2% annual levy on household net worth above $50 million, with a top rate she had raised that same month to 6% on fortunes above $1 billion to help pay for Medicare for All. Gates said he was not going to "make political declarations," and then made one anyway about the senator herself: "I'm not sure how open-minded she is. Or that she'd even be willing to sit down with somebody who has large amounts of money."

Sponsored Content: A $9 Trillion Flying Car Market Is Taking Shape. This Company Is Open to Investors.

Warren answered the next morning on Twitter. "I'm always happy to meet with people, even if we have different views," she wrote. "@BillGates, if we get the chance, I'd love to explain exactly how much you'd pay under my wealth tax. (I promise it's not $100 billion.)"

She was right about the $100 billion, at least on the first year's bill. Forbes and Bloomberg estimated Gates's fortune in November 2019 at around $107 billion. At a 6% top rate, Barchart's arithmetic puts the first annual payment near $6.4 billion, and the taxable fortune would shrink each year after that. At that pace, it would have taken well over a decade to reach the $100 billion he floated, before counting any investment gains on what remained. That is an estimate on a plan that was never enacted, and it is only as good as the net-worth figure it starts from.

The number Gates eventually chose to part with was larger than either of the ones he had joked about. On May 8, 2025, in a post on his Gates Notes blog titled "The last chapter of my career," he announced that the Gates Foundation would spend about $200 billion over the following two decades and close its doors on December 31, 2045. "People will say a lot of things about me when I die, but I am determined that 'he died rich' will not be one of them," he wrote. He said his own net worth would fall by 99% by the closing date. Bloomberg's Billionaires Index put that net worth at $108 billion the day of the announcement.

articles.title: JPMorgan's CEO sends a stern warning to corporate America
articles.summary: One of Wall Street’s most influential voices sees a problem that corporate America may not be ready for.
articles.body:
Jamie Dimon had a pointed question for corporate America.

Speaking to Bloomberg on Oct. 6 on the sidelines of a JPMorgan event in London, the bank's CEO asked whether companies, leveraged or not, are prepared for higher credit spreads when they have to refinance or borrow money.

Households would do well to ask themselves the same thing. Higher borrowing costs for companies tend to travel down the line to mortgages, car loans, and credit cards. Companies under pressure may also cut jobs or slow hiring to protect profits.

Dimon's warning is about competition for cash. He said the market will keep asking for more, and that at some point the pressure feeds into corporate debt and credit spreads.

His comments came during a global bond sell-off fed by the war in Iran and the AI boom's appetite for capital. That sell-off pushed the 10-year Treasury yield past levels last seen in 2002.

The AI boom is a big part of that demand. The four largest cloud companies are projected to spend about $725 billion on capital projects this year. That is up about 77% from 2025 and represents nearly all of their combined operating cash flow.

Goldman Sachs expects them to fund more than a third of their 2027 spending with debt, as reported by TheStreet .

That borrowing lands in the same pool of money the government taps. Dimon argues that tech companies building data centers are competing with the U.S. Treasury for the same funds. The national debt hit a record of about $40.25 trillion at the start of October, according to Moneywise .

Inflation is not helping either. Dimon described it as "the skunk at the party" in his April 6 shareholder letter, and said it could keep climbing in 2026 as the Iran conflict pushes energy costs higher. He also pushed back on the idea that AI spending is a bubble, writing that he does not see it that way.

JPMorgan's own strategists have spotted trouble in corporate debt. Leveraged loans trading below 60 cents on the dollar rose to $65 billion from $40 billion a year earlier. That is the most since March 2020, a jump of more than 60% in a year.

Technology companies make up a large share of the problem. The sector accounts for 39% of distressed loans.

The bank's strategists expect default rates on both high-yield bonds and leveraged loans to rise in 2027, Bloomberg reported . In all, 141 issuers had loans trading below 80 cents, 35 more than a year earlier.

articles.title: Bond Selloff May Mean Fewer Rate Hikes From Global Central Banks
articles.summary: Bond markets are starting to do some of the lifting for central banks around the world by pushing up borrowing costs themselves, potentially reducing the num...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Bond markets are starting to do some of the lifting for central banks around the world by pushing up borrowing costs themselves, potentially reducing the number of benchmark interest-rate hikes needed to get inflation under control.

Yields have surged to multiyear highs after weeks of selling, tightening financial conditions even without further action from policymakers. Traders have responded by paring rate-hike expectations, with the amount priced into swaps across eight major economies falling by almost 200 basis points since mid-September, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

There are few signs the bond selloff is abating as concerns over fiscal spending from the US to Japan and France push investors to demand more compensation, while a slew of AI-related debt issuance soaks up capital.

The higher borrowing costs are spilling into mortgages and junk credit, delivering some of the economic restraint central banks would otherwise seek through higher policy rates.

"The more tightening markets price, the tighter financial conditions become," said Ken Orchard, head of international fixed income at T. Rowe Price, which oversees $1.9 trillion. "And the tighter financial conditions become, the less tightening central banks may ultimately need — or be able — to deliver."

Traders are now pricing in a combined 539 basis points of rate hikes across the eight economies, down from 717 basis points in September, when expectations were the highest since 2022, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The biggest pullback has been in Australia, followed by the euro area amid concerns over France's fiscal outlook, then South Korea and Canada.

Red more: Europe's Indebted Nations Are Starting to Blink at Market Wrath

The average yield on global government bonds has climbed above 4% to the highest since 2000, raising the question of where the tipping point lies. Higher yields may do some of central banks' work for them, but if they appear too focused on bolstering growth, investors may doubt their commitment to fighting inflation and demand an even bigger premium to hold longer-dated debt.

"Central banks would ultimately have to balance the growth mandate with near-term inflation risk," said Yuxuan Tang, Asia head of rates and foreign-exchange strategy at JPMorgan Private Bank. "We think most rates markets are now overpricing the risk of further hikes, given the increasing downside risks to growth from the war's repercussions."

articles.title: China’s debt interest costs are soaring above U.S. levels and growing faster than any other budget category as Beijing struggles to prop up growth
articles.summary: China's spending on interest payments accounts for 19% of the central government’s general public budget and skyrocketed 341% between 2013 and 2025.
articles.body:
The world is flooded with debt, but while the U.S. and Europe have caused angst on global markets lately, China's fiscal situation isn't looking so great either.

In fact, China's debt has shot up so much in recent years that interest payments on all its borrowing are commanding a bigger share of public spending.

Debt-servicing payments will account for 19.2% of the central government's general public budget this year, up from 12% in 2014, according to new Conference Board estimates cited by the Financial Times .

That tracks with a separate report earlier this year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies , which also found that 19% of Beijing's spending is earmarked for interest on debt. That's more than the 14% of the U.S. federal budget that goes to interest costs, though less than Japan's 25.6%.

CSIS added that China's spending on interest payments skyrocketed 341% between 2013 and 2025, faster than any other major budget category. By comparison, total spending jumped 102% in that span, with outlays on social security and employment up 207%, science and technology up 137%, and defense up 141%.

To be sure, U.S. debt-interest spending looks grim too and has surged about 390% since 2013 to $1 trillion, which also tops the Pentagon's budget.

But the world's two biggest economies have been diverging in key ways with implications for future growth and indebtedness.

The U.S. economy is accelerating, helped by the AI boom, and despite high inflation, resilient consumers have continued to spend. Unemployment is low and signals full employment, while stock markets are at or near record highs.

Of course, hyperscalers are racing to issue bonds to fund their data centers and chip purchases, but they are also raising money with fresh stock offerings and IPOs.

Meanwhile, China's GDP has been decelerating and is on pace to undercut its annual target of 4.5%-5%. And while export-facing sectors are growing at a fast clip, trade partners are putting up barriers, Chinese consumers remain reluctant to spend, investment is weak, the property sector is still digging out from an epic crash, and Chinese stocks have been anemic.

Beijing has also steered state banks to provide financing to priority industries like electric vehicles, robotics, artificial intelligence and renewable energy.

But under pressure to lend, many loans went to questionable borrowers. Business debt has doubled since 2019, while revenues are only 30% higher. Creditors continue to roll over loans to keep struggling firms afloat, even as nearly a third of them are losing money.

articles.title: Nearly 70 million kids now have a Trump Account—but parents have to claim it first. Here’s who gets the $1,000
articles.summary: The Treasury auto-enrolled more than 60 million children, and $4.5 billion has flowed in since July. But the government’s seed money only goes to kids born f...
articles.body:
The Trump administration says nearly every child in America now has a Trump Account. Whether the money in those accounts ever adds up to much is a different question.

The Treasury Department announced Oct. 1 that it had finished automatically enrolling eligible children in the tax-advantaged investment accounts, creating accounts for more than 60 million kids who didn't already have one. Combined with the families who signed up on their own, that brings the total to nearly 70 million accounts, according to the White House .

"Today, I'm pleased to announce that every single eligible minor child in America has now been automatically enrolled in a Trump Account," President Donald Trump said at an Oval Office event on Oct. 7.

But having an account doesn't mean it's ready to use. A parent or guardian still has to claim it through the official Trump Accounts app before they can manage it, accept contributions from family and friends, or collect the government's $1,000 seed deposit for eligible children.

The switch to automatic enrollment followed slow uptake. Before the change, Treasury had processed about 5.6 million sign-up forms, less than a tenth of the roughly 73.4 million children eligible, InvestmentNews reported . Fortune previously reported that some families who signed up early were still waiting on their promised $1,000 .

Since the program launched on July 4, more than $4.5 billion has been deposited into Trump Accounts, including $1.3 billion in government seed contributions, more than $600 million from family and friends, and $2.6 billion in philanthropic gifts, according to the White House. Spread across nearly 70 million accounts, that averages out to about $64 per child.

Much of the philanthropic money comes from Michael and Susan Dell's $6.25 billion pledge, which provides $250 to up to 25 million children age 10 and under who live in ZIP codes with median household incomes below $150,000. More than 70 companies have also signed on to contribute to employees' children's accounts, the White House said, following early commitments from firms like JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America .

The administration has pitched the accounts as a path to serious wealth. The calculator on TrumpAccounts.gov projects that a lone $1,000 seed could grow to $243,000 by age 55, and that an account receiving the $5,000 annual maximum could reach $13 million. Those numbers assume the S&P 500 returns more than 10% a year without interruption for 55 years. Financial planners who spoke with Fortune put more conservative estimates at roughly $1.5 million to $2 million by 55 for a maxed-out account, assuming a 7% return.

images.caption: US President Donald Trump, alongside Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent (L), Susan Dell (2R), and Michael Dell (R), speaks about "Trump accounts," investment savings accounts for children, in the Oval Office in the White House in Washington, DC on October 7, 2026. · Fortune · Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images

articles.title: IKEA turns to driverless semis with nobody in the cab
articles.summary: Kodiak AI plans to haul IKEA freight on Texas highways with no one in the cab, raising urgent cybersecurity and safety questions for drivers.
articles.body: You could soon be driving down a Texas highway, look over at a massive delivery truck and realize the driver's seat is completely empty. Kodiak AI plans to start hauling IKEA products between the Dallas and Houston areas later this year with nobody in the cab. The company has spent years preparing for this step, but removing the safety observer changes the equation. What happens if something breaks while the truck is moving at highway speed? Is someone secretly driving it from a control room? How does it react to a police car or ambulance? And, yes, I wanted to know what keeps a hacker from getting anywhere near something as important as the steering or brakes. So, I took those questions directly to Kodiak founder and CEO Don Burnette to find out how the company says these driverless trucks will handle them. PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better healthcare. Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist. See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com. Why Kodiak believes it is ready to remove the driver "The decision to remove the driver isn't based on any single test or milestone," Burnette told CyberGuy. "It's the result of years of operating experience, rigorous validation and a clear safety case that gives us a clear, evidence-based framework for determining when the Kodiak Driver is ready to operate safely without anyone in the cab." Kodiak calls its autonomous driving system the Kodiak Driver. The company also uses something called an Autonomy Readiness Measure, or ARM, to track its progress toward running long-haul trucks without anyone aboard. As of the end of September, Kodiak said 96% of the claims and evidence required for its long-haul safety case were materially complete, up from 93% at the end of August. The remaining work includes engineering verification, validation and final safety assessments. Kodiak expects to complete that work before launching driverless long-haul service by the end of 2026. The company also has experience running trucks commercially with empty cabs. Kodiak-powered trucks have been operating for Atlas Energy Solutions in the Permian Basin without anyone aboard since December 2024. Burnette says that by the end of the second quarter, 35 driverless trucks were operating there commercially and had logged more than 40,000 hours of paid driverless operations. To put things in perspective, that is the equivalent of more than 4 ½ years of nonstop driving. So, the IKEA route will take Kodiak into a different setting, but removing the driver itself will not be new territory for the company. What changes when the IKEA driver comes out of the cab I asked Burnette what drivers on I-45 will actually notice once the new service starts. His answer was pretty straightforward. "The biggest difference is that there won't be anyone in the cab," he said. The driverless section will cover 219 miles, primarily along Interstate 45 between Kodiak facilities in the Dallas and Houston areas. That stretch is part of a longer 292-mile delivery route connecting IKEA's distribution center in Baytown with its store in Frisco. Kodiak has been carrying IKEA products along the route for four years with a safety observer aboard. During that time, the companies have also been figuring out the less obvious parts of running autonomous freight, such as when trucks should leave, when they will reach the destination and how maintenance should be scheduled. The trucks themselves have redundancy systems built into safety-critical components including braking, steering, power and computing. "From the outside, the drive itself should look pretty boring, and that's exactly what we want," Burnette said. "The Kodiak Driver is designed to be predictable, courteous, conservative and defensive." Frankly, boring is exactly what I think we all want from a giant truck with nobody sitting behind the wheel. What happens if something breaks while the truck is moving? This was high on my list of questions. "We've designed the Kodiak Driver around the idea that something will eventually go wrong, whether that's a mechanical issue, a damaged sensor or an unexpected situation on the road," Burnette said. "The important thing is that the truck already knows what to do when that happens." Burnette says the Kodiak Driver continuously monitors more than 1,000 safety-critical components across the truck, its sensors, hardware and autonomy software. If the system detects a serious issue, it can switch from normal driving into what Kodiak calls a fallback maneuver. That process is designed to bring the truck to a controlled stop in a safe location. Kodiak also puts limits around where and under what conditions the truck can operate. In the autonomous vehicle world, that is called an Operational Design Domain, or ODD. You can think of the ODD as the truck's approved operating boundaries. If the situation falls outside what the system has been designed and tested to handle, Burnette says the truck can fall back rather than continuing as though nothing has changed. DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES Is a person somewhere else remotely driving the truck? No one will be in the cab, but people will still be watching what is happening. Kodiak has a command center just south of Dallas. However, Burnette does not describe those workers as remote drivers waiting to take control. If the Kodiak Driver runs into a situation it cannot safely resolve, it can activate its fallback system and then, as Burnette puts it, "call home for help." The command center can provide guidance about what the truck should do next. That is different from a person taking over the steering wheel from miles away. "We use redundant communications channels to ensure we remain in contact with the truck, but if connectivity is lost, the Kodiak Driver still has to be able to respond safely on its own," Burnette said. That last part is especially important. If the cellular or communications connection goes down, the truck cannot simply sit there waiting for someone at the command center to tell it what to do. Kodiak says the vehicle still has to get itself into a safe state. What happens when police or an ambulance show up? Highway driving involves situations that go well beyond staying between the lane lines. Police pull vehicles over. Ambulances approach from behind. Accident scenes can suddenly change the flow of traffic. A truck with nobody in the cab still has to recognize what is happening around it and respond. Kodiak says its autonomous system is designed to identify emergency vehicles, stopped vehicles, lane closures and accident scenes. The system can slow down or move over when appropriate. The company has also spent time working directly with first responders. Kodiak employs a retired California Highway Patrol officer who works with law enforcement on how to interact with driverless trucks. The company also has a written First Responder Interaction Plan that explains what responders should do if they encounter one of its vehicles. Another piece of technology comes into play if a Kodiak truck stops along the road. Kodiak has integrated HAAS Alert's Safety Cloud. That system can send digital warnings about a stopped truck to nearby motorists through compatible navigation apps and vehicle systems. Could a hacker take over one of these driverless semis? You knew I was going to ask this one. Once software has control of an 18-wheeler, cybersecurity becomes a major part of the conversation. I asked Burnette what keeps someone from hacking into a truck and interfering with systems like the steering or brakes. "Cybersecurity is something we take very seriously," he said. Burnette says cybersecurity is one of six pillars in Kodiak's safety case. The company says its approach follows guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology and vehicle cybersecurity best practices from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. But the part that really stood out to me was how Burnette described limiting access to the truck. "First, we've minimized the number of ways into the truck," he said. "We limit data entry points to only what's necessary, and we isolate safety-critical functions like steering and braking from external communications." That isolation is important because communication with the outside world should not provide a direct doorway into critical driving systems. Burnette says Kodiak also monitors for threats and maintains an incident response process. Burnette also addressed what happens if the truck loses connectivity. "The truck's safety doesn't depend on connectivity, and it's designed to bring itself to a safe stop if something isn't right," Burnette said. No connected vehicle comes with a promise that hackers will never target it. That is why I will be watching how these protections hold up as more driverless trucks begin traveling public highways. AUTONOMOUS EXCAVATORS ARE DIGGING WITH EMPTY CABS Who is responsible if a driverless truck crashes? With a traditional truck, investigators can look at what the person behind the wheel did before a crash. But what happens when nobody was behind the wheel? I asked Burnette who would ultimately be responsible if a driverless Kodiak truck were involved in an accident. "Responsibility for a driverless vehicle works similarly to responsibility for any vehicle: it depends on the circumstances surrounding the crash," he said. Burnette says Kodiak trucks have more than a dozen sensors aboard. Those sensors can give the company a detailed record of what happened around the vehicle. That information could be especially useful when investigators need to reconstruct the moments leading up to a crash. What can a human truck driver still handle that the system cannot? I wanted to push on the limits too. Autonomous driving companies spend plenty of time telling us what their technology can do. I think it is just as useful to ask what it cannot do. Burnette pointed back to the Operational Design Domain. "The Kodiak Driver is designed to operate under specific conditions," he said. "If the truck leaves its ODD, it will simply achieve a fallback. That's intentional." At launch, Burnette says the ODD will cover the Dallas-Houston corridor. Kodiak plans to expand the operating area during 2027 and beyond. What does driverless trucking mean for truckers? This may be the biggest question of all for someone who makes a living driving a truck. If a semi can travel hundreds of highway miles without a person in the cab, what happens to the person who used to sit there? "We see autonomous trucks supplementing the workload rather than eliminating the need for them," Burnette said. Burnette also explained why Kodiak is targeting this type of work. "Our focus is on the long, repetitive highway miles that can keep drivers away from home for days or weeks at a time," Burnette told CyberGuy. There is still a much larger question about what happens if driverless freight eventually spreads across the country. Companies could change the way they divide routes and use drivers. Some jobs could change with them. We will know much more once autonomous trucking gets beyond a limited number of routes and starts becoming part of larger freight networks. Kurt's key takeaways The part I keep coming back to is that there will actually be nobody in the cab. Kodiak has spent four years hauling IKEA freight on this route with a safety observer aboard. Taking that person out changes the stakes, especially when you are talking about an 18-wheeler traveling alongside the rest of us on a busy interstate. I also give Burnette credit for answering our tougher questions. What happens when something breaks? Can somebody remotely drive it? How are the steering and brakes protected from hackers? Kodiak has built systems around each of those concerns, but now comes the test that counts. Once these trucks start piling up driverless highway miles with nobody there to step in, we will get a much clearer idea of how ready this technology really is. Would you feel comfortable driving next to an 18-wheeler with nobody behind the wheel, or would you keep your distance until driverless trucks have a much longer safety record? articles.title: Businesses Risk Wave of Democratic Probes on Costs, Corruption
articles.summary: Private businesses risk an onslaught of congressional investigations if Democrats prevail in midterm elections as the opposition party prepares to concentrat...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Private businesses risk an onslaught of congressional investigations if Democrats prevail in midterm elections as the opposition party prepares to concentrate sweeping oversight powers on allegations of Trump administration corruption and public anger over the cost of living.

Companies including Amazon.com Inc. and Nvidia Corp. have already been hit with investigative inquiries from Democrats who could compel testimony if the party secures a congressional majority.

"There's a cost to the American people of the out-of-control corruption that has been visited upon them by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries declared last month, as lawmakers left Washington for full-time campaigning. "We're going to hold the crooks accountable beginning on Day One."

Trump retains a veto over legislation for two more years, regardless of the election results. Not so over a new majority's oversight authority, which it can wield as a potent political weapon through attention-grabbing public hearings and damaging investigative revelations.

On consumer issues, key Democrats likely to gain subpoena power are showing continued interest in scrutinizing the party's perennial corporate punching bags in healthcare, tech, housing and financial services, as well as new targets related to surveillance pricing, data centers and artificial intelligence.

Companies and corporate executives also would be in the crosshairs of Democratic probes of Trump administration ethics controversies. Businesses perceived to have profited from ties to the White House would be targets — and with fewer legal privileges than the executive branch offer the quickest route to revelations that could ignite public outcry.

Amazon.com Inc., Apple Inc., Comcast Corp., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp. and Nvidia Corp. have already been hit with letters from Democratic lawmakers demanding information on donations to Trump's ballroom. Such letters typically telegraph investigative objectives.

Plenty of companies aren't waiting for the election to get ready.

"Many corporate clients, in particular, are acutely aware that there is a dark cloud looming on the horizon just past the beginning of November, and that there is going to be a broad wave of congressional investigations directed against Corporate America," said Robert Kelner, who leads Covington & Burling's congressional investigations practice.

articles.title: Are military hackers watching you through insecure cameras?
articles.summary:

articles.title: Diet soda drinkers lost just as much weight as water drinkers, study finds
articles.summary: Diet soda drinkers lost roughly the same amount of weight as water drinkers in a surprising long-term study.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — A recent study comparing British adults who drank either water or diet soft drinks while losing weight or maintaining their weight reached a surprising conclusion: There was essentially no difference between the two groups.

Researchers at the University of Liverpool tracked nearly 500 overweight or obese adults over two years and assigned participants to consume either water or a set amount of nonnutritive sweetened soft drinks each day.

Participants who drank beverages sweetened with aspartame , acesulfame-K or sucralose lost about the same amount of weight or maintained their weight at rates comparable to those who drank water. Both groups showed improvements in waist circumference, body composition and other metabolic measures, while also reducing their sugar intake.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomized trial,” Prof. Joanne Harrold, one of the researchers, said in a statement.

The study, published in the British Journal of Nutrition over the summer, was funded by the American Beverage Association, though researchers said their work was conducted independently.

While the findings could be viewed as a win for diet soda manufacturers, health professionals have historically expressed reservations about artificially sweetened beverages.

Many diet sodas contain caffeine, which is a diuretic , though generally not in amounts that would automatically cause dehydration. Studies have also suggested a potential link between artificial sweeteners and certain health conditions.

articles.title: GLP-1 combination therapy may unlock new benefits for psoriasis patients
articles.summary: The combination of medications also showed increased inflammatory immune activity compared with Taltz alone.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The latest research involving GLP-1 drugs suggests they may produce changes in adults with moderate-to-severe psoriasis and obesity .

New data from an Eli Lilly study found that adults with moderate-to-severe psoriasis and obesity experienced broader immune and metabolic changes when treated with both Taltz (ixekizumab) and Zepbound (tirzepatide) compared with Taltz alone.

“People living with psoriasis and obesity carry a compounded burden that extends beyond what is visible, yet these conditions are too often viewed through separate treatment lenses,” said Eli Lilly’s Dr. Mark Genovese, senior vice president of Lilly Immunology Development.

“The broader biomarker changes observed with Taltz and Zepbound, including those associated with skin clearance, may point to a meaningful relationship between immune and metabolic biology,” Genovese added.

Researchers measured circulating proteins and blood-based gene expression in patients and found that, by Week 36, those receiving the combination treatment showed greater changes in psoriasis-related, immune and metabolic biomarkers.

The combination therapy was associated with increases in 482 proteins and 467 genes, compared with 140 proteins and 16 genes in the Taltz-only group.

The medicine duo also showed increased inflammatory immune activity compared with Taltz alone.

“This analysis provides new insights into the potential connected immune and metabolic biology in people with psoriasis and obesity,” added Dr. James G. Krueger of The Rockefeller University.

Nearly 61 percent of Americans with psoriasis also have overweight or obesity and at least one obesity-related comorbidity, according to the data.

articles.title: Oil analyst ‘skeptical’ that Trump’s diesel deal with Russia will lower prices
articles.summary: Oil analyst Patrick De Haan said Monday that President Trump’s deal with Russia to supply the U.S. and global markets with diesel fuel may not lower fuel prices. “On the policy front, the Trump administration’s proposed diesel deal raises more questions than it answers, and I remain skeptical that it will deliver significant relief to…
articles.body:
Oil analyst Patrick De Haan said Monday that President Trump’s deal with Russia to supply the U.S. and global markets with diesel fuel may not lower fuel prices.

“On the policy front, the Trump administration’s proposed diesel deal raises more questions than it answers, and I remain skeptical that it will deliver significant relief to the trucking industry and consumers who depend on diesel,” De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote on the social platform X .

Trump said Friday that he and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to a deal under which Russia “will immediately supply” more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the American and global marketplaces.

Russia will supply another 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons “immediately thereafter” and 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” depending on the condition of its diesel refineries, Trump added.

“Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” the president wrote Friday on Truth Social.

Ukrainian forces have targeted Russian oil refineries recently, as its four-year war against Russia marches on.

Trump claimed Sunday the two sides reached an energy ceasefire deal , although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said later in the day that Russian forces attacked a power plant in Kharkiv, Ukraine.

Diesel prices have spiked amid the U.S.-Iran and Ukraine-Russia conflicts. The national average price of a gallon of diesel fuel is roughly $6.27 as of Monday, roughly $2.60 higher than a year ago, according to data from AAA .

De Haan noted Monday diesel prices have decreased slightly in the last week, as AAA reports the per-gallon cost dipped by about 5 cents.

Regular gas, which costs roughly $4.36 per gallon as of Monday, is also down by roughly 1 cent week to week. Gas prices are still up by about $1.28 from a year ago, according to AAA.

“For now, the trend is cautiously in the right direction for motorists, but between hurricane season and continued geopolitical uncertainty, it is far too early to declare the pressure on fuel prices resolved,” De Haan said.

images.caption: Diesel prices are seen at a Sheetz in Linthicum Heights, Md., on Oct. 6, 2026.
